title: The Burdock Burrs That Became Velcro
description: A Swiss engineer gets curious about why burdock burrs cling so fiercely to his dog's fur after a countryside walk, and spends years turning that question into a fastener. Rejected by clothing makers at first, his invention only takes off once NASA needs something to keep gear from floating away in space.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: Did you know the strip that holds your shoes shut was copied from a weed, and that nobody wanted it until NASA came looking? This is the story of Velcro, and of the nearly twenty years one Swiss engineer spent teaching a burr to work for him. It begins in Switzerland in 1941. George de Mestral comes back from a hunting trip in the countryside to find his trousers covered in burrs, the round prickly seed pods of the burdock plant, and his dog's coat is just as bad, hundreds of them stuck deep in the fur. Most people would just pick them off and forget about it. He wanted to know why they held on so stubbornly, and that question would not leave him alone.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: De Mestral pulled a few burrs off his dog and put them under a microscope. What he saw was not glue and not sap. It was structure. Every burr was covered in hundreds of tiny hooks, each one curved just enough to catch on the small loops in woven fabric, or in the loops of a dog's fur. Nothing sticky at all, just hooks finding loops and holding on until something pulled them apart. He thought if nature could build a fastener like that, he could build one too, out of two strips, one covered in tiny hooks and one woven with tiny loops, pressed together to hold and pulled apart to release.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: The loop side was easy to weave. The hook side nearly beat him. A hook had to be stiff enough to grip but flexible enough to let go, and no fabric he knew of could do both. He carried the idea from one fabric plant to another across Europe and was turned away again and again, until a manufacturer in Lyon pointed him toward nylon, a material that held its shape through thousands of bends the way the others could not. He patented the idea in 1955, borrowed a hundred and fifty thousand dollars, and even then the hooks could only be cut by hand, one at a time, far too slow to sell.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: He shut himself in a small cabin in the Swiss village of Commugny, in the Alps, trying to solve one stubborn detail, the angle of the cut that turned a woven loop into a working hook. The answer came from watching barbers' clippers, which hold a blade at a steady angle as it moves. Built into a loom, that same steady angle let him cut thousands of identical hooks at once. Nearly twenty years after the walk with his dog, he finally had a machine that could make his fastener by the mile.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: Even with the machine working, nobody wanted it at first. Manufacturers had buttons and zippers and saw no reason to change, and for years de Mestral's fastener sat around looking like a clever idea going nowhere. Then NASA, working out how to keep tools and food from drifting off in zero gravity, started using it, and the fastener that had failed to impress tailors suddenly looked like the future. Fashion followed, with designer Pierre Cardin putting it into his clothing by the mid-1960s. He called it Velcro, from the French for velvet and hook, and it now closes shoes, jackets, and spacecraft equipment, all traced back to a dog covered in burdock on a walk in 1941. Follow for more stories from science. Until next time, stay curious.
